newsitem.title: USA: US House Democrats unable to agree on own tax plan.
newsitem.headline: US House Democrats unable to agree on own tax plan.

text.p: House Democrats on Tuesday were unable to agree on which of three competing tax plans to offer as an alternative to a Republican proposal to cut taxes by $85 billion over five years.
The Democrats met late in the day with the intent of approving a tax cut plan to rival the one put forward Monday by House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer, a Texas Republican.
The legislation aims to fill in the tax details of the balanced budget agreement reached last month between congressional leaders and the White House.
But after being presented with three alternatives, the Democratic caucus found its members divided and will revisit the issue again Wednesday.

House Democratic Leader Richard Gephardt of Missouri said he still expected a Democratic tax bill would be offered in the House Ways and Means Committee, which is scheduled to start consideration of Archer's bill Wednesday.

"One of the outrages here is that we're having to do this so quickly, I mean it would be nice if we had a little more time," Gephardt said. "To have this thing dropped on us one day and you've got to vote the next, that doesn't make a lot of sense," he said.

Rep. Charles Rangel of New York, the ranking Democrat on the House tax-writing panel, has proposed a tax cut plan that would allocate half of the package to education tax initiatives and a child tax credit.

It would also provide targeted capital gains tax relief for small businesses and homeowners. Rangel's proposal would not scale back the ethanol tax subsidy nor would it tax Indian tribe gaming, as Archer has proposed. It would extend the airline ticket tax.

"I'm asking whether or not he (Archer) could see his way clear to review the objections that the president has made over the bill and to give us an opportunity to amend it so that possibly we could reach a bipartisan closure on this," Rangel said.

Rep. Collin Peterson, a Democrat from Minnesota and co-chair of the conservative "Blue Dog" Democrats, said his group's tax proposal would end up with about $50 billion left over of a $250 billion net tax cut over 10 years that was part of the budget agreement. The leftover amount would go toward further deficit reduction, he said.

Peterson said the plan included a capital gains tax cut, President Clinton's education tax initiatives, a $500 child tax credit only if that amount was put into a savings-type account, and an increased threshold at which the estate tax kicks in of $1.2 million from the current $600,000.
"We have more money than we can spend," Peterson said in an interview.
The third Democratic proposal was offered by Rep. Jim McDermott of Washington, who is a member of the Ways and Means Committee.
His proposal would return to workers two percent of the first $20,000 in wages. In essence, anyone earning that amount or higher would get $400 a year back.

"You want to give a tax break to the working people who need it? this does it," McDermott said. "It doesn't make any difference if you have kids, you're married, not married -- if you're working, you get $400 back," he said.
